The formula assumes returns reinvested and constant periodic interest.

entries.title: Present value (discounting)
entries.summary: Present value = future amount ÷ (1 + discount rate)^periods.
entries.details: At 10% for 10 years, the multiplier is ≈ 0.3855 (the table rounds to .386). The textbook’s Table 1-5 provides a range of rates and periods, but the formula permits direct calculation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 26–27
entries.laymanExplanation: Present value asks how much money today is equivalent to a larger amount promised in the future.
entries.legalExplanation: Discount future cash with PV = FV/(1+r)^n. Table 1-5 gives the present-value factor 0.386 for 10 years at 10%; a $10,000 future receipt therefore has a rounded present value of $3,860, versus the direct-calculation result of approximately $3,855.43. The book's factors are approximations and do not create a legal tax rule.

entries.title: After-tax compounding without deferral
entries.summary: Initial after-tax principal = principal × (1 − tax rate); annual after-tax growth uses return × (1 − tax rate).
entries.details: The chapter compares an immediate 40% tax and annual taxation of 10% yields with delayed taxation. This is a simplified model that assumes a constant rate and full annual taxation of investment returns.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 26
entries.laymanExplanation: If taxes are collected from investment earnings every year, less money remains invested and compounding may be reduced.
entries.legalExplanation: Under the textbook's simplified model with $10,000 gross funds, a 40% immediate tax leaves $6,000 to invest; 10% interest taxed annually at 40% leaves a 6% after-tax growth rate. Ten-year result = $6,000(1.06)^10 ≈ $10,745. By contrast, prefunded deferral permits $10,000(1.10)^10(0.60) ≈ $15,562 after the tax paid at withdrawal. Twenty-year results are approximately $19,243 without deferral and $40,365 with deferral. These are fixed-rate comparisons only.
entries.examApplication: Compute both after-tax terminal amounts at 10 and 20 years using the source's 10% return and 40% tax assumptions; compare, then discuss how a different future rate changes the result.
entries.examTrap: Deferred tax at a higher future marginal rate may negate the modeled advantage.

topics.title: E. Compliance, Audits & Litigation
topics.description: Self-assessment, assessment procedures, penalties and forum choice.

entries.title: Self-assessment and payment reconciliation
entries.summary: Taxpayers calculate liability; withholding and estimated payments are credited toward that liability.
entries.details: The IRS administers returns, matching, audits, and collections. After computing tax and credits, compare tax owed against taxes already paid to determine remaining balance or refund.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 28
entries.laymanExplanation: You usually calculate and report your own tax on a return. Withholding and estimated tax payments reduce what remains to pay, or may create a refund.
entries.legalExplanation: The personal federal income tax primarily uses annual self-assessment: the taxpayer determines income and deductions, files the return, and compares computed liability with withholding and estimated tax installments already paid. Excess prepayments generally result in a refund; an underpayment results in tax due. Separate filing and information-reporting obligations support IRS enforcement.

entries.title: Audit and deficiency
entries.summary: Audit is closer IRS scrutiny; deficiency is an asserted amount of underpaid tax.
entries.details: The general assessment period discussed by the textbook is three years, subject to major exceptions. Interest typically accrues on underpayments; penalties may also apply. The IRS often resolves disputes administratively.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 28–29
entries.laymanExplanation: An audit is an IRS check of your return. A deficiency is the additional tax the IRS says you owe.
entries.legalExplanation: An audit is a closer IRS examination of a return. The textbook introduces a general three-year period for the IRS to assert a deficiency, with statutory exceptions including certain omitted income and false or fraudulent returns. An underpayment may accrue statutory interest separately from civil penalties; the actual interest rate is set under Code provisions rather than remaining fixed at one percentage.

entries.title: Tax litigation forum choice
entries.summary: Tax Court generally permits qualifying prepayment deficiency challenges; refund suits generally follow payment.
entries.details: Tax Court: no jury, specialist judges, appeal to regional circuit. Federal district court: refund litigation after payment, jury potentially available, regional circuit appeal. Court of Federal Claims: refund litigation after payment, Federal Circuit appeal. Procedural requirements and deadlines are important and not fully covered in the introductory summary.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 29
entries.laymanExplanation: The court you use for a tax dispute matters. Some cases can be contested in Tax Court before paying the proposed deficiency; refund cases generally involve paying first.
entries.legalExplanation: Tax Court offers a common prepayment deficiency forum for eligible taxpayers with a valid notice and timely petition; it conducts bench trials with specialized tax judges and appeals usually to the appropriate geographic circuit. In contrast, ordinary refund suits in district courts and the Court of Federal Claims generally require paying and satisfying refund-claim prerequisites. District court may have a jury; Court of Federal Claims appeals to the Federal Circuit. These are introductory comparisons and do not replace procedural statutes.
entries.examApplication: Choose Tax Court for an appropriate prepayment deficiency challenge, or a paid-refund forum after meeting jurisdictional and claim prerequisites. Explain court/jury/appeal differences.
entries.examTrap: A refund case and a deficiency petition have different payment, jurisdictional and timing requirements.

entries.title: Accuracy-related civil penalties
entries.summary: The casebook describes a 20% penalty for specified negligence/substantial-understatement underpayments.
entries.details: The chapter notes substantial authority, adequate disclosure/reasonable basis, and reasonable-cause/good-faith rules that may limit penalties. Multiple overlapping 20% grounds generally do not simply stack. Check current §6662/§6664 and exact facts.
entries.source: IRC §§ 6662, 6664; Bankman et al. pp. 29–30
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax mistakes can trigger civil penalties, not just extra tax. The applicable penalty and possible defenses depend on what went wrong.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §6662, negligence and substantial-understatement grounds can produce a 20% accuracy-related penalty on the portion of underpayment attributable to the specified ground. The reading discusses reduction based on substantial authority or adequately disclosed positions with reasonable basis and potentially reasonable-cause/good-faith protection under §6664. The same portion of an underpayment does not automatically incur multiple 20% penalties for overlapping grounds.
entries.examApplication: Identify the statutory penalty ground and potentially qualifying substantial-authority, disclosure or reasonable-cause defense; do not merely multiply any error by 20%.

entries.title: Failure-to-file, failure-to-pay, and fraud penalties
entries.summary: The chapter lists monthly filing/payment penalties and a 75% civil-fraud penalty.
entries.details: As a basic introductory reference: failure to file is generally 5% per month up to 25%; failure to pay generally 0.5% per month up to 25%, with statutory interactions and exceptions. Civil fraud generally can produce a 75% penalty on the fraud portion. Actual computation depends on relevant rules and dates.
entries.source: IRC §§ 6651, 6663; Bankman et al. p. 30
entries.laymanExplanation: Filing late, paying late, and deliberately committing fraud are different violations with different penalties.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook introduces generally applicable late-filing penalties of 5% per month (up to 25%) and late-payment penalties of 0.5% per month (up to 25%), subject to statutory adjustment and interaction. Fraud-related civil penalties can reach 75% of the tax underpayment attributable to fraud. Identify the precise taxable event, deadline, return status and statutory exceptions before performing a penalty calculation.

entries.title: Criminal tax evasion
entries.summary: Willful tax evasion can create felony exposure in addition to civil sanctions.
entries.details: The casebook contrasts civil and criminal enforcement and describes a six-year limitations period for specified tax offenses. Criminal liability requires the relevant statutory elements and mental state.
entries.source: IRC §7201; Bankman et al. p. 30
entries.laymanExplanation: Criminal tax evasion is more than getting a tax number wrong: it involves intentional conduct to evade tax under the governing criminal requirements.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal criminal tax evasion under §7201 requires willful attempted evasion or defeat of a tax imposed under the Code or its payment; the source describes criminal sanctions and a six-year criminal limitations period for specified offenses. Criminal tax liability has distinct intent and proof requirements beyond ordinary civil deficiency or negligence.

entries.title: Tax underpayment, deficiency, and assessment
entries.summary: An underpayment concerns unpaid tax; a deficiency is a statutorily defined additional liability asserted through deficiency procedures; assessment formally records the IRS's tax claim.
entries.details: For exam purposes identify the proposed deficiency, assessment, possible administrative review, interest and payment procedure. The Chapter 1 introductory discussion simplifies these distinctions; full statutory definitions and notice procedures appear elsewhere in the Code.
entries.laymanExplanation: A deficiency notice means the IRS believes you owe more than your return showed. Assessment is the government's formal recording of a tax amount for collection.
entries.legalExplanation: For exam purposes identify the proposed deficiency, assessment, possible administrative review, interest and payment procedure. The Chapter 1 introductory discussion simplifies these distinctions; full statutory definitions and notice procedures appear elsewhere in the Code.
entries.source: Assigned Class 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 28–29

entries.title: Substantial understatement and penalty defenses
entries.summary: A substantial understatement may trigger §6662 accuracy-related penalties, but the Code recognizes specified substantial-authority, disclosure, and reasonable-cause rules.
entries.details: The textbook introduces a 20% accuracy-related penalty and identifies circumstances relevant to reducing the understatement or qualifying for reasonable-cause/good-faith protection. Tax year, taxpayer type, applicable authority, reasonable basis, and disclosure must be assessed before deciding penalty liability.
entries.laymanExplanation: Making a big tax mistake can carry an extra penalty. But the law may treat a reasonable, disclosed position differently from careless reporting.
entries.legalExplanation: The textbook introduces a 20% accuracy-related penalty and identifies circumstances relevant to reducing the understatement or qualifying for reasonable-cause/good-faith protection. Tax year, taxpayer type, applicable authority, reasonable basis, and disclosure must be assessed before deciding penalty liability.
entries.source: Assigned Class 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 29–30

topics.title: F. Sources of Federal Tax Law
topics.description: Hierarchy and practical use of tax statutes, regulations, case law, IRS guidance.

entries.title: Start with the Internal Revenue Code
entries.summary: Federal tax liability must rest on statutory authority; statutory text is the starting point.
entries.details: Read the controlling provision, definitions, cross-references, and exceptions. Follow regulations, binding case law, and pertinent IRS guidance, while considering how judicial doctrines deal with substance over form.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 30–31
entries.legalExplanation: Federal income-tax liability begins with enacted Code provisions. Statutory definitions, cross-references and exclusions should be reviewed first; then applicable regulations, judicial decisions and published IRS guidance. The reading stresses that courts also use substance-over-form reasoning and law-like doctrines where statutory language is incomplete or susceptible to manipulation.

entries.title: Legislative history and JCT
entries.summary: Committee reports and Joint Committee on Taxation materials help explain statutory purposes.
entries.details: Tax-writing committees: House Ways and Means and Senate Finance. JCT staff work on legislative analysis and official revenue estimates; JCT 'blue books' summarize legislation after enactment. These are aids to interpretation, not substitutes for enacted law.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 31
entries.legalExplanation: Legislative history can help interpret uncertain provisions. House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committee reports may explain complex drafting compromises; Joint Committee on Taxation staff assists and prepares revenue estimates and 'blue books' summarizing enacted laws. These explanatory documents are not themselves statutes.

entries.title: Treasury regulations under §7805
entries.summary: Treasury issues regulations interpreting and implementing the Code.
entries.details: The textbook discusses Mayo (2011) and Chevron deference as the then-governing doctrine. CURRENT-LAW UPDATE: Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron; courts independently interpret law under the APA. A delegation to an agency can remain legally relevant; the old automatic ambiguity-triggered Chevron rule is not current.
entries.source: IRC §7805; Mayo Foundation v. United States (2011); Loper Bright v. Raimondo (2024)
entries.alert: OUTDATED IN CASEBOOK: Chevron deference was overruled in 2024.
entries.laymanExplanation: Treasury regulations are detailed rules issued by Treasury that help explain how the Internal Revenue Code operates.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 7805 authorizes Treasury to issue regulations for Code enforcement, and particular provisions may specifically delegate regulatory tasks. Income-tax regulations generally use the '1.' number series and proposed regulations ordinarily undergo applicable notice-and-comment procedures. The casebook's description of Chevron deference after Mayo reflects the doctrine as it stood in 2011; the Supreme Court's Loper Bright decision (2024) overruled Chevron's mandatory ambiguity-based deference, while statutory delegations may still matter.
entries.examApplication: Start with a Code section, then the regulation, then relevant binding case law; if Chevron is invoked from the casebook, state that Loper Bright later changed judicial interpretive deference.
entries.examTrap: Do not write that a court must follow any reasonable Treasury interpretation simply because the statute is ambiguous; that is the overruled Chevron approach.

entries.title: Revenue Rulings and Revenue Procedures
entries.summary: Rev. Rul. expresses IRS legal position on a fact pattern; Rev. Proc. addresses administration/procedures.
entries.details: Both are IRS guidance, generally less authoritative than duly issued Treasury regulations and judicial precedent. Their practical importance is substantial, but authority and reliance depend on the specific type and context.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 32
entries.laymanExplanation: Revenue rulings explain the IRS's position on how law applies to facts. Revenue procedures generally explain processes and administrative rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Revenue Rulings express the IRS's published position on how a law applies to a given set of facts; Revenue Procedures describe IRS administrative practices and processes. They are important to practitioners but do not have the same status as Code text or properly promulgated Treasury regulations.
entries.examApplication: Classify the source of guidance in a tax research question. Do not treat an unpublished PLR as general binding authority.

entries.title: Private Letter Rulings (PLRs)
entries.summary: IRS written advice to a particular taxpayer generally may not be cited as precedent by others.
entries.details: PLRs can reveal the Service’s likely approach but do not create general binding law. Distinguished from published Revenue Rulings.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 32–33
entries.laymanExplanation: A private letter ruling is the IRS answering a particular taxpayer's question. Other taxpayers generally cannot treat that letter as binding precedent.
entries.legalExplanation: A PLR responds to a specific taxpayer's factual ruling request. Although letter rulings may illuminate IRS analysis, under §6110(k)(3) a written determination generally cannot be used or cited as precedent by other taxpayers. The reading differentiates PLRs from public Revenue Rulings stating an IRS position with broader applicability.

entries.title: Tax Court decisions and IRS acquiescence
entries.summary: Tax Court has regular and memorandum decisions; IRS may announce acquiescence or nonacquiescence.
entries.details: Acquiescence signals internal acceptance of a ruling for similar cases; nonacquiescence signals continued disagreement and possible relitigation. Neither itself reverses binding judicial precedent.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), pp. 33
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax Court decisions interpret tax law. The IRS may say whether it accepts a particular decision's reasoning for similar cases.
entries.legalExplanation: The Tax Court publishes regular opinions and memorandum decisions, and the IRS sometimes announces whether it acquiesces or nonacquiesces in adverse opinions. Acquiescence indicates an administrative willingness to follow the decision in similar matters; nonacquiescence indicates disagreement and possible relitigation, subject to binding appellate rulings. The source's Golsen footnote explains the importance of the circuit of appeal.

entries.title: Cited authority: Mayo Foundation (2011) — old Chevron framework
entries.summary: Historical: applied Chevron framework to Treasury regulations.
entries.details: The textbook uses Mayo to describe the then-prevailing standard. It is useful for historical understanding, but Chevron was overruled in Loper Bright (2024).
entries.alert: Historical doctrinal treatment; not a statement of the current Chevron standard.

legalWarning.label: FRAMEWORK OVERRULED
legalWarning.reason: Mayo applied Chevron deference to Treasury regulations. Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron's mandatory deference framework. This does not mean every holding previously relying on Chevron was automatically overturned; Mayo is useful for tracing the former approach.

entries.legalExplanation: Mayo Foundation (2011) was cited by the casebook as applying Chevron-style agency deference to Treasury tax regulations. The subsequent Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024) decision overruled that mandatory deference framework. The case is mentioned here as an example, not reproduced as an assigned judicial opinion, so it belongs in supporting doctrine with an updated-law warning.

entries.title: Cited authority: Eisner v. Macomber (1920)
entries.summary: Historical case used to introduce unrealized appreciation and constitutional income questions.
entries.details: The chapter contrasts unrealized appreciation with income. Subsequent decisions limit simplistic formulations; Moore v. United States (2024) did not decide whether realization is always constitutionally required.
entries.source: 252 U.S. 189 (1920); Moore v. United States, 602 U.S. 572 (2024)
entries.alert: Do not treat the casebook’s brief historical description as a complete modern constitutional rule.

legalWarning.label: HISTORICAL — QUALIFIED
legalWarning.reason: Eisner v. Macomber is an important historical decision on realization, but do not treat its broad language as a complete statement of today's constitutional tax law. Moore v. United States (2024) expressly left the general realization requirement unresolved.

entries.legalExplanation: Eisner v. Macomber (1920) is referenced as a historical example concerning realization of gains and constitutional conceptions of income. Its narrow income-from-capital-or-labor phrase is not a complete current definition, as later discussed in Glenshaw Glass. Modern constitutional realization questions also require careful attention to holdings and unresolved issues; this is a supporting citation in Chapter 1, not a reproduced assigned opinion.

entries.title: Substance over form
entries.summary: A judicial interpretive principle that evaluates the real economic substance of a transaction rather than relying solely on its legal label or paperwork.
entries.details: The source emphasizes that courts can disregard arrangements whose form complies with literal words but whose substance conflicts with the operation of tax law. Do not treat it as permission to ignore clear statutory terms; identify the governing rule and why the underlying economic arrangement matters.
entries.laymanExplanation: Calling a payment a 'loan' or a 'gift' doesn't automatically make it one. Tax law can look at what actually happened.
entries.legalExplanation: The source emphasizes that courts can disregard arrangements whose form complies with literal words but whose substance conflicts with the operation of tax law. Do not treat it as permission to ignore clear statutory terms; identify the governing rule and why the underlying economic arrangement matters.
entries.source: Assigned Class 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 30–31

entries.title: Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) and 'blue books'
entries.summary: Congressional tax-policy staff who assist with drafting, estimate revenue effects and summarize enacted tax legislation.
entries.details: The Joint Committee staff works with House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees. Their official revenue estimates commonly address a 10-year horizon, and explanatory 'blue books' are informative but are not enacted tax law.
entries.laymanExplanation: JCT experts help Congress calculate how much a proposed tax change would raise or cost, and publish useful explanations afterward.
entries.legalExplanation: The Joint Committee staff works with House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees. Their official revenue estimates commonly address a 10-year horizon, and explanatory 'blue books' are informative but are not enacted tax law.
entries.source: Assigned Class 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 31

entries.title: Reading Treasury regulation citations
entries.summary: Income-tax Treasury regulations typically use a section number beginning '1.' followed by the related Code section; other subject areas use different title prefixes.
entries.details: The source gives Reg. §1.170-1 (charitable contributions) and estate-tax Reg. §20.2041-1 as examples. It also discusses proposed regulations, Federal Register publication and comments under the Administrative Procedure Act.
entries.laymanExplanation: When you see Reg. §1.170-1, the number 170 tells you it relates to Code §170. The '1.' signals the income-tax regulation series.
entries.legalExplanation: The source gives Reg. §1.170-1 (charitable contributions) and estate-tax Reg. §20.2041-1 as examples. It also discusses proposed regulations, Federal Register publication and comments under the Administrative Procedure Act.
entries.source: Assigned Class 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 31–32

entries.title: Golsen rule (Tax Court appellate precedent)
entries.summary: The Tax Court generally follows the controlling precedent of the court of appeals to which a particular case would be appealed.
entries.details: The casebook notes that when the Tax Court disagrees with an appellate circuit's rule, it generally still follows that circuit for a case appealable there. Golsen v. Commissioner is cited in a note, not reproduced as an assigned judicial opinion; no separate case brief is appropriate.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even if Tax Court judges would prefer a different interpretation, they generally follow the appeals court whose jurisdiction covers that taxpayer's case.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook notes that when the Tax Court disagrees with an appellate circuit's rule, it generally still follows that circuit for a case appealable there. Golsen v. Commissioner is cited in a note, not reproduced as an assigned judicial opinion; no separate case brief is appropriate.
entries.source: Assigned Class 1, Bankman/Shaviro/Stark/Scharff, Federal Income Taxation, 19th ed., Ch. 1, printed pp. 33

topics.title: A. Why Tax Income?
topics.description: Ability-to-pay rationale and competing tax bases.

entries.title: Ability to pay
entries.summary: A principle for allocating tax burdens based on a taxpayer's economic capacity, rather than equal dollar charges.
entries.details: Income is a practical but imperfect proxy; ability to pay need not equal immediate cash liquidity. A broader endowment concept would consider earnings potential, but is generally not taxed.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 36
entries.laymanExplanation: The basic fairness idea is that someone with greater financial resources may reasonably be expected to contribute more in taxes.

entries.title: Head tax (capitation)
entries.summary: A fixed dollar amount charged to each person, without regard to earnings, wealth, or spending.
entries.details: The reading uses it to contrast economic efficiency with perceived unfairness. The 2022 $17,500 example is historical, not an actual tax.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 35
entries.laymanExplanation: Imagine everyone owes the same $10,000 tax regardless of income. Easy to calculate, but extremely hard on people who earn little.

entries.title: Tax base
entries.summary: The economic amount or activity used to measure and calculate tax; examples include income, consumption, and wealth.
entries.details: Choosing a base determines which economic opportunities or transactions get taxed; income may not capture leisure or untapped earning capacity.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 36
entries.laymanExplanation: Taxing wages, spending, and wealth are different ways to pick what gets measured before a tax rate is applied.

entries.title: Endowment / wage rate
entries.summary: A person's potential hourly earning capacity, even if they choose not to exercise it.
entries.details: Dora and Felix each earn $52,000 annually, but work 50 and 10 hours per week respectively. An income tax sees the same pay, not the opportunity cost of differing leisure.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 36
entries.laymanExplanation: Two people may earn the same paycheck, but one works far fewer hours. Their ability to earn per hour can differ even if income tax treats their earnings alike.

entries.title: Haig–Simons income
entries.summary: Economic income equals consumption plus the change in net worth over a specified period.
entries.details: Broader economic benchmark than statutory gross income: includes appreciation in wealth even where realization-based tax rules may defer inclusion.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 37
entries.elements: Y = C + ΔW, where C = market value of consumption and ΔW = change in net worth.
entries.laymanExplanation: This economist's definition says your income is what you consume plus how much richer you became during the period. It's broader than what today's tax return necessarily counts.

entries.title: Haig–Simons income calculation
entries.summary: Income = consumption + saving, equivalently consumption + change in net worth.
entries.details: If wages are $10,000, consumption $9,000 and saving $1,000, then Y=$10,000. If consumption is $11,000 and borrowing increases by $1,000, change in net worth is −$1,000 and Y remains $10,000.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 37
entries.laymanExplanation: If you spent $9,000 and saved another $1,000, the formula says you had $10,000 of economic income. Saving and spending are two destinations for income.

entries.title: Consumption tax
entries.summary: A levy measured by resources used for consumption rather than those saved and invested.
entries.details: A cash-flow version can generally be understood as income with a deduction for saving and inclusion when saved/borrowed funds are used for consumption.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 38
entries.laymanExplanation: A consumption tax focuses on what you use or spend, rather than taxing money simply because you earned and saved it.

entries.title: Imputed income
entries.summary: Economic value generated by goods or services one provides to oneself, such as living in one's own home or performing unpaid household services.
entries.details: The textbook discusses why ordinary income-tax administration largely ignores much imputed income, despite economic similarities to market transactions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 38
entries.laymanExplanation: If you fix your own house rather than paying someone else, you receive something valuable without getting paid money. Economists can view that unpaid benefit as income.

entries.title: Why tax income instead of equal head taxes?
entries.summary: The ability-to-pay rationale supports differential burdens despite efficiency costs.
entries.details: The chapter asks whether taxes should also measure leisure, wage capacity, valuation, administrability, and fairness.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 35

topics.title: B. What Counts as Gross Income?
topics.description: IRC §61, Glenshaw Glass, found cash and windfalls.

entries.title: IRC §61 — Broad inclusion of gross income
entries.summary: Gross income includes all income from whatever source derived, unless another provision excludes it.
entries.details: §61(a) lists examples without limiting the overall definition. Source or label of payment alone does not control inclusion; examine statutory exclusions separately.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 39
entries.examApplication: For any receipt, identify the actual benefit, who controls it, whether it is realized, and any asserted Code exclusion.
entries.examTrap: The absence of a specific item in §61's illustrative list does NOT establish exclusion.
entries.laymanExplanation: When something valuable comes in, the starting point is that it counts as income. You need a legal reason to leave it out.

entries.title: Windfall
entries.summary: An unexpected economic gain not necessarily earned through labor or investment.
entries.details: A windfall can still be taxable. The textbook contrasts a narrow early formulation of income with Glenshaw Glass and later found-property cases.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 40
entries.laymanExplanation: A windfall is money or value you unexpectedly receive, like money found in a piano. Unexpected does not mean tax-free.

entries.title: Glenshaw Glass accession-to-wealth formulation
entries.summary: Gross income reaches undeniable accessions to wealth, clearly realized, over which the taxpayer has complete dominion.
entries.details: This is the landmark framework derived from the reproduced Glenshaw Glass opinion; punitive damages generally qualify as taxable gross income.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 42
entries.examTrap: Do not universalize Eisner v. Macomber's older income-from-capital-or-labor phrase.
entries.laymanExplanation: The Court's basic idea: if you genuinely gain wealth, actually receive or realize it, and control it, you're generally dealing with income.

entries.title: Cesarini v. United States
entries.summary: Yes. Found cash is taxable as treasure trove in the year reduced to undisputed possession; the taxpayers were not entitled to their claimed refund.
entries.details: Assigned excerpt: the reproduced court opinion, not merely an incidental citation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 43
entries.facts: A couple bought a used piano in 1957 for about $15. In 1964, they found $4,467 in old currency inside it and initially included that amount in gross income. They filed an amended return claiming a refund.
entries.issue: Does cash discovered inside a purchased piano constitute taxable gross income, and in what year?
entries.holding: Yes. Found cash is taxable as treasure trove in the year reduced to undisputed possession; the taxpayers were not entitled to their claimed refund.
entries.reasoning: §61 and Treas. Reg. §§1.61-1(a) and 1.61-14(a) broadly include gains from any source. The found cash was not covered by an exclusion; it was not an excludable gift under §102 simply because §61 did not list treasure trove.
entries.rule: For found cash or other treasure, identify when the finder obtains undisputed possession, determine its value, and include it in gross income absent an exclusion.

exam.source: Cesarini v. United States, 296 F. Supp. 3 (N.D. Ohio 1969), reproduced in assigned Chapter 2 pp. 43–45

examApplication.source: Cesarini v. United States, 296 F. Supp. 3 (N.D. Ohio 1969), reproduced in assigned Chapter 2 pp. 43–45

entries.laymanExplanation: A couple found cash hidden inside a used piano years after buying it. The court treated the money as taxable when it became theirs to keep, rather than as a tax-free surprise.

entries.title: Treasure trove
entries.summary: Found money or property that may generate gross income when reduced to undisputed possession.
entries.details: Treas. Reg. §1.61-14(a), relied upon in Cesarini, includes treasure trove at its U.S.-currency value in the year of undisputed possession.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 45
entries.laymanExplanation: Treasure trove means valuable property or money someone finds. Once the finder has undisputed possession, its value can be taxable.

entries.title: Eisner v. Macomber as cited in Glenshaw Glass
entries.summary: The older capital-and-labor definition did not govern all future gross-income questions.
entries.details: Glenshaw Glass explains that the earlier decision concerned stock dividends and realization, not a universal exclusion for windfalls.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 40

legalWarning.label: OLDER FORMULATION LIMITED
legalWarning.reason: Glenshaw Glass rejected treating Macomber's phrase as a universal definition of gross income.

entries.title: Gross income — punitive damages
entries.summary: Punitive damage recoveries are generally included in gross income under the broad statutory definition of income, absent an applicable exclusion.
entries.details: The Court read § 22(a) of the 1939 Code (predecessor of § 61) broadly: Congress did not restrict gross income to earnings from productive labor, capital, or conventional transactions.
entries.source: Commissioner v. Glenshaw Glass Co., 348 U.S. 426 (1955), excerpt supplied, pp. 40–42
entries.examApplication: Determine whether the receipt represents a realized accession to wealth subject to the taxpayer's control. Punitive nature alone is not an exclusion.
entries.examTrap: Do not treat punitive damages as automatically untaxed windfalls.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lawsuit payout does not become tax-free simply because it punishes the defendant. Punitive damages can count as income.

entries.title: Commissioner v. Glenshaw Glass Co.
entries.summary: The Supreme Court held that punitive damages recovered in litigation constitute gross income under the broad federal income-tax statute.
entries.facts: Glenshaw Glass received a settlement from Hartford-Empire; $324,529.94 was allocated to punitive damages for fraud and antitrust violations, which Glenshaw did not report as income. In the consolidated Goldman Theatres matter, a treble-damages award totaled $375,000: Goldman reported only the $125,000 compensatory portion, excluding the $250,000 punitive balance. The Tax Court and Third Circuit sided with the taxpayers.
entries.issue: Are punitive damages for fraud or antitrust violations taxable as gross income under § 22(a) of the 1939 Code, predecessor of § 61?
entries.holding: Yes. Punitive damages are gross income. The Supreme Court reversed the favorable decisions below.
entries.reasoning: Congress used expansive language — income from whatever source derived — to tax gains unless specifically excluded. Punitive payments are undeniable accessions to wealth, clearly realized, and under the taxpayers' complete dominion. Their punitive source does not alter their status as income. The Court rejected using the narrower Eisner v. Macomber phrasing as a universal test for gross income because that case addressed whether a stock dividend was a realized gain.
entries.rule: Undeniable accessions to wealth, clearly realized, and over which taxpayers have complete dominion, generally fall within gross income unless a specific exclusion applies.
entries.exam: For unfamiliar receipts, analyze the breadth of § 61 and the Glenshaw Glass accession-to-wealth formulation; separately assess any applicable exclusion. Do not infer that punitive damages are excluded simply because they punish wrongdoing.
entries.examApplication: Hypothetical: A business receives $125,000 to compensate lost profit and $250,000 in punitive antitrust damages. Under the opinion's statutory construction, both amounts fall within gross income, absent an applicable exclusion.
entries.examTrap: The Court did not hold that every transfer or increase in asset value is necessarily taxable at once; realization and exclusions still matter.
entries.source: User-provided reproduced opinion, Commissioner v. Glenshaw Glass Co., 348 U.S. 426 (1955), pp. 40–42. Case brief summarizes only the supplied excerpt.
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced judicial opinion supplied by user — dedicated assigned case brief.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two companies kept the punitive part of lawsuit recoveries off their tax returns. The Supreme Court said those payments still increased their wealth and were taxable.

topics.title: C. Noncash Benefits & Employee Fringe Benefits

entries.title: Noncash compensation is generally income
entries.summary: Income realized in money, property, or services can be included in gross income; payment in kind is not automatically exempt.
entries.details: Treas. Reg. §1.61-1(a). When services are paid for with property, generally include the fair market value of property received as compensation under Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1).
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 46
entries.examApplication: A lawyer performs services in exchange for renovations. Analyze the fair market value of services/property received rather than treating the barter as tax-free.
entries.laymanExplanation: Getting paid with groceries, services, a car, or other property doesn't automatically avoid income tax. The value of what you receive can still be pay.

entries.title: Fringe benefit
entries.summary: Compensation or other employee benefit received without cash, or at a below-market price.
entries.details: Includes employer meals, lodging, insurance, discounts, travel, parking and access to facilities. Analyze inclusion under §61 and any specific exclusions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 59
entries.laymanExplanation: A fringe benefit is a perk from your employer in addition to ordinary wages—like free meals or travel.

entries.title: Fair market value (FMV)
entries.summary: Value property or services would command in an arm's-length market transaction.
entries.details: General benchmark for valuing taxable noncash fringe benefits under Reg. §1.61-21(b), potentially subject to special valuation methods.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 61
entries.laymanExplanation: Fair market value is roughly the price a willing buyer and seller would agree on in an ordinary market deal.

entries.title: IRC §119 — Meals furnished for employer convenience
entries.summary: Employer-provided meals may be excluded when furnished for the employer's convenience on its business premises.
entries.details: Unlike lodging, meals under §119 do not separately require acceptance as a condition of employment. Employer convenience and on-premises furnishing matter.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 52
entries.elements: (1) Meals furnished by/on behalf of employer; (2) for employer's convenience; (3) on employer's business premises; (4) qualifying employee/family recipient.
entries.examTrap: Cash allowances are not necessarily meals furnished. Distinguish paid cash from food furnished.
entries.laymanExplanation: Free meals at work can be tax-free when the employer provides them for genuine work-related reasons at the workplace, not just as extra pay.

entries.title: IRC §119 — Lodging furnished for employer convenience
entries.summary: Employer-provided lodging may be excluded if furnished for employer convenience, on business premises, and employee is required to accept it as a condition of employment.
entries.details: The statutory exclusion has more stringent elements for lodging than meals.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 52
entries.elements: (1) Lodging furnished by/on behalf of employer; (2) employer convenience; (3) business premises; (4) employee required to accept as condition of employment.
entries.examTrap: Being provided free housing does not itself prove the employer-convenience or employment-condition requirements.
entries.laymanExplanation: Free housing from your employer may be tax-free only if it is provided for work reasons, at the workplace, and you must live there to perform the job.

entries.title: Benaglia v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Board held the meals and lodging were not income where provided solely for the employer's convenience rather than compensation.
entries.details: Assigned excerpt: the reproduced court opinion, not merely an incidental citation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 48
entries.facts: Benaglia managed Hawaiian resort hotels and, with his wife, lived and ate at a hotel for work. The Commissioner added $7,845 annually as FMV of room and board.
entries.issue: Whether employer-provided lodging and meals were taxable compensation when necessary for the hotel manager's duties.
entries.holding: The Board held the meals and lodging were not income where provided solely for the employer's convenience rather than compensation.
entries.reasoning: The hotel manager's continuous presence was practically necessary to perform the job. The dissent argued the employment contract made meals and rooms compensation and they had economic value. Congress later adopted a specific statutory rule in §119.
entries.rule: Apply today's §119 tests to a hotel manager or similar worker; use Benaglia for the historical development of the convenience-of-employer principle.

exam.source: Benaglia v. Commissioner, 36 B.T.A. 838 (1937), reproduced at pp. 48–51

legalWarning.label: STATUTORY RULE NOW CONTROLS
legalWarning.reason: Benaglia is an assigned historical opinion; Congress later codified a more specific rule in §119 (1954). Apply §119 on current-law exams.

examApplication.source: Benaglia v. Commissioner, 36 B.T.A. 838 (1937), reproduced at pp. 48–51

legalWarning.label: STATUTORY RULE NOW CONTROLS
legalWarning.reason: Benaglia is an assigned historical opinion; Congress later codified a more specific rule in §119 (1954). Apply §119 on current-law exams.

entries.laymanExplanation: A hotel manager had to stay at the hotel to do his job. The court viewed the meals and room as provided for the employer's needs, not as ordinary extra pay. Modern exams apply the statute, §119.

entries.title: United States v. Gotcher
entries.summary: The business-purpose portion of the husband's trip was not income; his wife's vacation-oriented trip provided a taxable personal economic benefit.
entries.details: Assigned excerpt: the reproduced court opinion, not merely an incidental citation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 56
entries.facts: A Volkswagen dealer and his wife took a twelve-day trip to Germany funded principally by Volkswagen. The dealer toured facilities and met with relevant personnel; his wife's trip had a more personal vacation character.
entries.issue: Whether the expense-paid trip was income to the dealer and his spouse under §61.
entries.holding: The business-purpose portion of the husband's trip was not income; his wife's vacation-oriented trip provided a taxable personal economic benefit.
entries.reasoning: Economic gain and primary benefit to the payor matter. The record suggested the husband effectively had to attend to advance dealership interests, while the wife largely enjoyed a vacation.
entries.rule: Separate who benefits from employer-sponsored travel, business purpose, and personal consumption; analyze spouses separately.

exam.source: United States v. Gotcher, 401 F.2d 118 (5th Cir. 1968), reproduced at pp. 56–59

examApplication.source: United States v. Gotcher, 401 F.2d 118 (5th Cir. 1968), reproduced at pp. 56–59

entries.laymanExplanation: A car dealer's company-funded factory trip mainly served the business, but the spouse's vacation-like trip benefited her personally. The court treated them differently.

entries.title: IRC §132 — No-additional-cost services
entries.summary: Qualifying services provided to employees that cause no substantial additional cost may be excludable.
entries.details: Example: an otherwise empty seat for an airline employee on a flight, subject to employer's line-of-business and nondiscrimination rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 60
entries.laymanExplanation: If letting an employee use a spare airline seat costs the airline almost nothing extra, the perk may fit a special tax exclusion.

entries.title: IRC §132 — Qualified employee discounts
entries.summary: Employee discounts on goods or services ordinarily sold in the employer's line of business may qualify for exclusion within statutory limits.
entries.details: Line-of-business and nondiscrimination restrictions apply to this benefit category.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 60
entries.laymanExplanation: Employees sometimes get tax-favored discounts on the goods or services their employer normally sells, up to legal limits.

entries.title: IRC §132 — Working-condition fringe
entries.summary: An employee may exclude an employment-related benefit that would be deductible as a business expense if the employee had paid for it.
entries.details: Examples from reading: qualifying business use of a company automobile and industry subscriptions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 60
entries.laymanExplanation: If the employer pays for something you'd properly deduct as a business expense yourself, the perk may be excluded as a working-condition fringe.

entries.title: IRC §132 — De minimis fringe
entries.summary: Benefits so small in value or infrequent that accounting is unreasonable or administratively impracticable can be excluded.
entries.details: Separate rules address certain eating facilities; this category is not a blanket exclusion for recurring valuable perks.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 60
entries.laymanExplanation: Tiny or occasional workplace perks may not be worth tracking for tax purposes; major recurring perks aren't automatically 'de minimis.'

entries.title: IRC §132 — Other fringe categories
entries.summary: Qualified transportation fringes, retirement-planning services and certain on-premises athletic facilities may qualify for specific exclusions.
entries.details: Different statutory limitations and eligible recipients apply; do not assume every benefit can be extended tax-free to family members.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 60
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax law has additional special rules for certain transit benefits, retirement-planning help, and on-premises gyms.

entries.title: IRC §125 — Cafeteria plans
entries.summary: A qualifying cafeteria plan allows an employee to choose between taxable cash and specified tax-favored benefits without automatic taxation solely because cash was available.
entries.details: Without statutory protection, the constructive-receipt doctrine could tax the available cash choice. Coverage and nondiscrimination limitations apply.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 62
entries.laymanExplanation: A cafeteria plan lets workers choose among specified benefits and cash without making all the qualified benefit choices taxable just because cash was available.

entries.title: Constructive receipt
entries.summary: Tax doctrine potentially treating income as received when unrestrictedly made available despite the taxpayer's choice not to take it.
entries.details: The chapter references this doctrine to explain why §125 cafeteria plans need express statutory authorization; full timing rules occur later.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 62
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't always avoid income tax by refusing money that's already available to you. Tax law may treat it as received anyway.

entries.title: Use-it-or-lose-it rule
entries.summary: Certain cafeteria-plan amounts designated for eligible expenses may be forfeited if not used within permitted periods.
entries.details: The chapter illustrates the planning burden; specific carryover and grace-period exceptions should be checked under current plan rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 62
entries.laymanExplanation: Some benefits money must be spent on eligible expenses within set time limits, or you may lose unused amounts, subject to plan exceptions.

entries.title: Employer-provided health coverage — §§105–106
entries.summary: Qualifying employer-paid health insurance and certain reimbursements for medical care can be excluded under specific statutes.
entries.details: The text describes employer-paid medical insurance, medical expense reimbursements, and the role of §125 health FSA arrangements; verify specific statutory requirements.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 63
entries.laymanExplanation: Employer medical insurance and certain medical reimbursements often receive favorable tax treatment under special rules.

entries.title: Turner v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The court used an amount lower than the stated retail ticket value, recognizing valuation difficulty for the particular benefit.
entries.details: Assigned excerpt: the reproduced court opinion, not merely an incidental citation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 64
entries.facts: Reginald Turner answered questions on a radio program and won two restricted, nontransferable first-class steamship tickets. Their retail price was $2,220. The couple reported $520. They exchanged the tickets plus $12.50 for four tourist-class tickets and took a family trip.
entries.issue: What amount of gross income must the winning couple include for restricted cruise tickets awarded as a prize?
entries.holding: The court valued the prize at $1,400, below the $2,220 retail price and above the $520 reported.
entries.reasoning: The first-class tickets were restricted, nontransferable and not ordinarily something the taxpayers would purchase. Their economic value was less than retail, though the taxpayers did obtain substantial vacation benefits.
entries.rule: Taxable noncash prizes are included at an appropriate value; restrictions and practical marketability can affect valuation.
entries.exam: Distinguish taxable receipt from proper valuation; describe the factual basis for adjusting retail FMV where prize transferability and actual use are constrained.

examApplication.source: Turner v. Commissioner, 13 T.C.M. 462 (1954), reproduced in assigned Chapter 2 pp. 64–67

entries.laymanExplanation: Someone won expensive travel tickets they couldn't easily sell. The court did not simply use the full ticket price; it looked at what the benefit was realistically worth.

entries.title: Why fringe-benefit exclusions exist
entries.summary: Valuation, business purpose, fairness, enforcement cost and historical practice help explain special exclusions.
entries.details: Google employer meals, frequent flyer miles, business entertainment, and valuation debates are optional policy context.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 54

entries.title: IRC §107 — Ministers' housing exclusion
entries.summary: Qualifying ministers may exclude specified employer-furnished parsonage rental value or eligible housing allowance, within statutory limits.
entries.details: §107(1) excludes the rental value of a furnished parsonage provided as compensation. §107(2) excludes a qualifying designated housing allowance used for the home, limited by fair rental value including furnishings, related property and utilities. IRS guidance also limits allowance exclusion to the amount designated in advance and actually spent. Housing allowance generally remains subject to self-employment tax.
entries.source: IRC §107; IRS Ministers' Compensation and Housing Allowance FAQ; Gaylor v. Mnuchin (assigned PDF)
entries.elements: Compare the housing allowance officially designated in advance, the amount actually used to provide a home, and the home's fair rental value with furnishings and utilities; subject to qualifications.
entries.examTrap: Distinguish income-tax exclusion from self-employment tax treatment and §107(1) furnished housing from §107(2) cash allowances.
entries.laymanExplanation: A qualifying minister may be able to exclude certain employer-provided housing or a designated housing allowance from income tax, within limits.

entries.title: Gaylor v. Mnuchin
entries.summary: The Seventh Circuit held §107(2)'s clergy housing-allowance exclusion did not violate the Establishment Clause, reversing the district court.
entries.facts: Freedom From Religion Foundation employees and their organization challenged the income-tax exclusion for qualifying clergy housing allowances under IRC §107(2). A district court ruled the exemption unconstitutional; the government and religious organizations appealed.
entries.issue: Did §107(2)'s tax exclusion for clergy housing allowances violate the First Amendment's Establishment Clause, and did the challengers have standing?
entries.holding: The plaintiffs had standing, but §107(2) did not violate the Establishment Clause. The Seventh Circuit reversed the district court's judgment.
entries.reasoning: The court examined the historical tradition of religious tax accommodations, comparable housing exclusions in the Code, secular administrative convenience, denominational neutrality, and avoiding excessive entanglement. Applying then-prevailing Establishment Clause reasoning, including Lemon-related analysis and historical practices, it found the exemption constitutionally permissible.
entries.rule: A legislative tax accommodation for religious housing does not inherently violate the Establishment Clause; Gaylor upheld §107(2) based on its statutory context, religious neutrality, and historical practice.
entries.exam: If challenged tax exclusion for clergy housing, identify §107(2), address standing, apply constitutional limits and distinguish the Seventh Circuit's holding from later Supreme Court changes to Establishment Clause methodology.
entries.examApplication: Analyze whether a qualified minister's designated housing allowance is excluded under §107(2) and, separately, whether the statute itself survives Establishment Clause scrutiny.
entries.examTrap: Gaylor remains an important decision, but do not apply the old Lemon test as the current governing Establishment Clause framework following Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022).
entries.details: This opinion was provided separately as an 18-page Federal Reporter PDF. Its excerpt includes the Federal Reporter headnotes and surrounding cases; the dedicated brief is only for Gaylor v. Mnuchin, not adjacent cases printed on the same pages.
entries.source: User-supplied Gaylor opinion (1).pdf, 919 F.3d 420–437 (7th Cir. 2019)
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced assigned judicial opinion supplied as a separate PDF

legalWarning.label: METHOD UPDATED AFTER 2019
legalWarning.reason: Gaylor's result upholding §107(2) should be distinguished from its use of Lemon-era Establishment Clause analysis. Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022) stated that courts should use historical practices and understandings instead of Lemon and the endorsement test.
legalWarning.authority: Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch. Dist., 597 U.S. 507 (2022)

entries.laymanExplanation: A group challenged a tax break for clergy housing. The appeals court said that the statutory exclusion was constitutional; later Supreme Court cases changed the test courts use for these church-and-state disputes.

topics.title: D. Recovery of Capital
topics.description: Basis and capital-recovery doctrine, wagering losses and reimbursements.

entries.title: Return of invested capital is not gross income
entries.summary: Amounts that merely return a taxpayer's capital (tax basis) are not income; gain generally arises only beyond the taxpayer's recoverable basis.
entries.details: Repayment of the same $500 loan principal, or sale of $500-basis stock for $500, produces no gain. Distinguish receipts representing earnings from recoveries of investment.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
entries.examTrap: Gross proceeds are not automatically the same as taxable gain.
entries.laymanExplanation: Getting back money you already invested is not a new profit. If you lend $500 and receive $500 back, that principal repayment is not income.

entries.title: Basis
entries.summary: A taxpayer's unrecovered tax investment in an asset, ordinarily its cost, subject to statutory adjustments.
entries.details: Basis prevents taxing recovery of one's own investment as though it were income. Reference §§ 1011, 1012, 1016 as developed in the course.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
entries.laymanExplanation: Your basis is your tax 'starting cost' in property. It matters because you usually pay tax on profit above that cost, not the whole sale price.

entries.title: Amount realized
entries.summary: Consideration received on disposition of property, measured under the governing realization rules.
entries.details: In a simple cash sale, amount realized is sale proceeds; gain is amount realized minus adjusted basis, subject to transaction-specific rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
entries.laymanExplanation: Amount realized is what you get when you sell property, before subtracting the property's tax basis to figure out gain.

entries.title: Realized gain or loss from disposition
entries.summary: Realized gain (loss) = amount realized − adjusted basis.
entries.details: Simple example: sell stock for $700 with allocated adjusted basis $400 → $300 realized gain. The character and recognition of the result require additional analysis.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
entries.examApplication: Always identify adjusted basis before measuring gain, and separate gain amount from recognition and characterization.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sell something for $700 with $400 in basis: the difference, $300, is your realized gain.

entries.title: Allocate basis when part of property is sold
entries.summary: When an asset or acquired block of property is partly disposed of, reasonably apportion cost basis among the interests disposed of.
entries.details: For 100 shares acquired for $1,000, 40 identical shares have $400 allocated basis. For nonuniform land, allocate by relative value rather than acreage alone where appropriate.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 69
entries.laymanExplanation: If you sell only part of something, you have to work out how much of your original purchase cost belongs to the part sold.

entries.title: Basis allocation
entries.summary: The assignment of a portion of total cost to property or rights separately sold or disposed of.
entries.details: The book contrasts homogeneous stock with wooded and tillable acreage. An impossible/impracticable allocation may warrant special treatment under Inaja.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 69
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't always divide a property's basis simply by the number of acres or shares; what each portion was worth may matter.

entries.title: Inaja Land Co. v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Tax Court treated the net $49,000 as a tax-free return of capital reducing the property's basis, because reliably allocating basis to the affected property rights was impracticable and the payment was below total basis.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 69
entries.facts: The taxpayer bought 1,236 acres and water rights for $61,000. The City of Los Angeles caused flooding and sediment damage, then paid $50,000 for easements and release of claims; legal costs were $1,000, producing a net $49,000 receipt.
entries.issue: Was the $49,000 payment taxable income or return of capital, and must basis be allocated to the easements?
entries.holding: The Tax Court treated the net $49,000 as a tax-free return of capital reducing the property's basis, because reliably allocating basis to the affected property rights was impracticable and the payment was below total basis.
entries.reasoning: The payment compensated for property rights and damage, not lost profits. Ordinarily a partial sale requires cost allocation, but a gain cannot be calculated on conjecture unsupported by ascertainable facts.
entries.rule: Identify the character of a settlement; if paid for property rights, attempt reasonable basis allocation. Only if allocation is truly impracticable analyze the Inaja exception and reduce remaining basis.

exam.source: Inaja Land Co. v. Commissioner, 9 T.C. 727 (1947), excerpt reproduced pp. 69–70

examApplication.source: Inaja Land Co. v. Commissioner, 9 T.C. 727 (1947), excerpt reproduced pp. 69–70

entries.laymanExplanation: A landowner was paid for damage and easement rights. The court allowed the payment to reduce property basis because nobody could reasonably assign a precise cost to the rights surrendered.

entries.title: IRC §165(d) — Wagering losses (2026)
entries.summary: For 2026 taxable years, wagering-loss deduction equals at most 90% of wagering losses, capped by wagering gains.
entries.details: The casebook describes an older loss-to-gains offset. Current §165(d), effective 2026, limits the deduction to the lesser of 90% of losses or gambling gains. The book's discussion of sessions and nonprofessional itemizing requires attention to applicable-year facts.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 72
entries.elements: Allowable wagering loss deduction = min(90% × total wagering losses, total wagering gains), subject to other applicable rules.
entries.examTrap: Do not use the textbook's pre-2026 full-loss offset for a 2026 tax-year problem without checking the test's assigned law.

legalWarning.label: 2026 STATUTE CHANGED
legalWarning.reason: The book states gambling losses are deductible up to gambling winnings; for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, Pub. L. 119-21 changed §165(d) to a 90% allowable-loss formula capped by winnings.

entries.laymanExplanation: For tax year 2026, the book's old rule for gambling losses changed: even if you lose as much as you win, you may not be able to deduct all of the losses.

entries.title: Basketing / scheduling rules
entries.summary: Rules that allow losses or deductions to offset only income in a specified category, rather than income generally.
entries.details: Chapter examples: wagering losses (§165(d)), capital losses (§1211), passive losses (§469), hobby-related limits (§183), investment interest (§163(d)).
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 72
entries.laymanExplanation: Some losses can only be used against gains of the same kind. Picture separate baskets for different categories of tax items.

entries.title: Gambling session
entries.summary: A grouping concept used in determining amounts won and lost during a related gambling session.
entries.details: The text distinguishes in-session netting from separately incurred losses, particularly for nonprofessional taxpayers who itemize.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 72
entries.laymanExplanation: A gambling session means a defined period of betting. The way wins and losses are grouped can affect tax calculations.

entries.title: Clark v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Board ruled for the taxpayer: the $19,941.10 reimbursement compensated for a loss rather than yielding taxable income.
entries.details:
The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.

Related syllabus handout: The government's 2018 McKenney appellate brief distinguishes Clark's unnecessary tax overpayment from reimbursement of legally owed tax. The 2020 Eleventh Circuit opinion is separately identified as follow-up research; do not confuse the brief with a court opinion.
entries.source: Clark v. Commissioner, 40 B.T.A. 333 (1939), assigned excerpt pp. 74–75
entries.facts: Tax counsel negligently prepared the taxpayer's joint return. He paid more federal income tax than he would have owed using a properly advised separate-return election. Counsel reimbursed $19,941.10, representing that excess tax expense; the IRS asserted the reimbursement was gross income.
entries.issue: Is reimbursement of a non-deductible overpayment caused by counsel's negligence taxable income?
entries.holding: The Board ruled for the taxpayer: the $19,941.10 reimbursement compensated for a loss rather than yielding taxable income.
entries.reasoning: The taxpayer paid his own tax; counsel did not discharge an existing liability for him. The court treated reimbursement as restoration of a lost amount. Its reliance on the narrow old capital/labor definition is outdated, but the textbook says the limited holding survives.
entries.rule: A reimbursement restoring nondeducted, unnecessarily lost capital may be excluded under Clark's narrow facts; distinguish payments for loss of an expected tax saving or normal business-transacting costs.
entries.exam: Ask whether the payment merely replaces an excess amount actually paid because of negligent preparation, and whether any deduction previously created a tax benefit.
entries.examApplication: Ask whether the payment merely replaces an excess amount actually paid because of negligent preparation, and whether any deduction previously created a tax benefit.

legalWarning.label: OLD REASONING NO LONGER LAW
legalWarning.reason: The reading expressly states Clark's 'derived from capital or labor' rationale is no longer good law after Glenshaw Glass, though its narrow reimbursement holding remains.
legalWarning.authority: Glenshaw Glass; textbook's Current Legal Status of Clark note

entries.laymanExplanation: An accountant's mistake caused a taxpayer to pay more tax than legally necessary. The accountant paid him back. The court treated that reimbursement as making him whole, not extra income.

entries.title: Recovery of loss
entries.summary: Receipt that restores a prior economic loss rather than adding new net wealth, potentially raising tax-benefit and basis questions.
entries.details: The text compares Clark's tax overpayment to an asset having recoverable basis; treatment may depend on whether an earlier deduction was taken.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 75
entries.laymanExplanation: If you lose $100 and later get that same $100 back, you may simply be recovering what you lost rather than making a new profit. The exact tax result depends on earlier deductions and the type of loss.

entries.title: Tax benefit doctrine (preview)
entries.summary: A later recovery may be included in income to the extent an earlier deduction reduced tax.
entries.details: Introduced through the lost-pay-envelope hypothetical and addressed in more detail in a later chapter.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 77
entries.laymanExplanation: If a loss reduced your taxes last year and you later get that money back, the recovery may have to be included in income to undo the earlier tax advantage.

entries.title: Clark fairness paradox
entries.summary: One reimbursed overpayer is better off than an uncompensated overpayer, but merely equal to a taxpayer who never overpaid.
entries.details: The text uses this to illustrate how tax rules define the relevant transaction and may leave some economic inequities.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 76

entries.title: Actual tax liability versus tax overpayment
entries.summary: An actual tax liability is tax legally owed on the transactions undertaken; an overpayment is tax paid beyond that liability. Do not equate a potentially better tax strategy with an overpayment.
entries.details: In the government's 2018 McKenney brief, the McKenneys agreed with the IRS in a closing agreement that they owed approximately $2.2 million additional taxes for 2000–2005. They later obtained an $800,000 settlement from their accounting firm. The government argued that this recovered part of taxes actually owed, not tax they had overpaid through erroneous return preparation. The brief distinguishes an actual historical transaction from hypothetical, more favorable tax planning; these are the government's arguments, not the court's decision.
entries.examApplication: Compare Clark: Did the accountant cause payment beyond the taxpayer's actual legally correct tax, or did the taxpayer pay tax actually owed on the chosen transaction and later receive money from the accountant?
entries.examTrap: Tax that could have been avoided through a different transaction is not automatically an overpayment of tax actually owed. Keep the party's argument separate from a judicial holding.
entries.source: Assigned 'McKenny brief handout (1).pdf', five pages: government's redacted opening brief, Eleventh Circuit No. 18-10810, filed Sept. 6, 2018 (original appellate-brief pp. 21–24). This is government advocacy, not a judicial opinion.
entries.sourceRole: Definition and exam distinction derived from the government's assigned brief, not an attributed court holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: There is a difference between paying too much tax by mistake and paying the correct tax on a deal that turned out to be a bad tax-saving idea.

entries.title: Old Colony principle — third-party payment of a taxpayer's tax
entries.summary: When another party pays a taxpayer's legally owed federal income tax on the taxpayer's behalf as a benefit, the discharge of that liability can constitute taxable income.
entries.details: The government's McKenney brief invoked Old Colony Trust Co. v. Commissioner, 279 U.S. 716 (1929), to argue that an accountant's settlement effectively reimbursing valid tax obligations should be included under §61. The handout does not reproduce the Old Colony judicial opinion, so Old Colony remains supporting cited authority, not a dedicated case brief. Whether a particular damages recovery is taxable also requires analysis of what the payment replaces.
entries.examApplication: Identify the underlying taxpayer liability and what a third-party payment actually reimburses. Contrast legal discharge or reimbursement of taxes owed with replacement of an amount paid unnecessarily because of a negligent filing choice.
entries.examTrap: Do not apply Old Colony automatically to all malpractice recoveries; Clark's actual-overpayment facts and the nature of the claimed loss may matter.
entries.source: Assigned 'McKenny brief handout (1).pdf', five pages: government's redacted opening brief, Eleventh Circuit No. 18-10810, filed Sept. 6, 2018 (original appellate-brief pp. 21–24). This is government advocacy, not a judicial opinion.
entries.sourceRole: Legal principle cited in the government's assigned brief; the case opinion is not reproduced in the handout.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your employer or another person pays a tax bill you actually owe for you, that can be the same as receiving money to pay it yourself.

entries.title: Assigned supplemental advocacy — United States' brief in McKenney
entries.summary: The government argued an $800,000 accountant-malpractice settlement was taxable because it reimbursed valid tax liabilities, unlike the excess tax payment in Clark.
entries.details:
DOCUMENT TYPE: Government's redacted opening appellate brief filed September 6, 2018, not a judicial opinion.

FACTS AS ARGUED: Joseph and Amy McKenney used S corporations owned by an ESOP to structure consulting and dealership income. After examination, they signed a closing agreement accepting an IRS determination concerning an abusive ESOP transaction and acknowledged approximately $2.2 million in additional taxes for 2000–2005. They later settled malpractice claims against Grant Thornton for $800,000.

GOVERNMENT'S POSITION: The $800,000 replaced part of tax liabilities the taxpayers actually owed, and thus was income under §61 and Old Colony Trust. It distinguished Clark because Clark involved an accountant reimbursing tax actually overpaid. It also argued that tax consequences should follow transactions actually entered, not hypothetical restructuring that would have saved tax.

LIMITATION: These are arguments made by one litigant. The excerpt does not contain judicial findings or a court's holding. A 2020 court decision is separately linked in the current-law notes.
entries.examApplication: Exam comparison: Clark taxpayer overpaid due to erroneous filing advice; McKenney taxpayers' accountant advised transaction design and the government treated the additional tax on that actual transaction as legally owed. Explain why that difference matters for characterizing the settlement, while keeping the source's advocacy status clear.
entries.examTrap: Never cite the 2018 brief itself as the Eleventh Circuit's holding. The brief includes one party's characterization of the facts and the law.
entries.source: Assigned 'McKenny brief handout (1).pdf', five pages: government's redacted opening brief, Eleventh Circuit No. 18-10810, filed Sept. 6, 2018 (original appellate-brief pp. 21–24). This is government advocacy, not a judicial opinion.
entries.sourceRole: Assigned appellate advocacy excerpt — NOT a reproduced judicial opinion.

legalWarning.label: PARTY BRIEF — NOT A HOLDING
legalWarning.reason: This PDF contains the government's September 2018 advocacy, not an appellate decision. The Eleventh Circuit later ruled in September 2020; its outcome appears as separately researched follow-up, not as content of the assigned handout.
legalWarning.authority: McKenney v. United States, No. 18-10810 (11th Cir. Sept. 1, 2020)

topics.title: E. Personal & Business Injury Recoveries
topics.description: Character of damages, §104(a)(2), deferred settlements and constitutional questions.

entries.title: Business lost-profit damages are income
entries.summary: Amounts recovered to replace profits that would have been taxable are generally included in income.
entries.details: Settlement or insurance proceeds can be analyzed by what they replace; punitive damages also generally fall within §61.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: If a business gets money to replace profits it missed out on, the payment is generally treated much like the profits would have been.

entries.title: Damages for destroyed business property — basis recovery
entries.summary: Recovery for damaged or destroyed property generally produces gain to the extent proceeds exceed adjusted basis; §1033 may permit qualifying deferral.
entries.details: Example from reading: $700,000 recovery for a building with $600,000 basis results in $100,000 gain absent qualifying nonrecognition.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: If a destroyed building had $600,000 of tax basis and you receive $700,000 for it, the extra $100,000 can be gain, unless another rule postpones recognizing it.

entries.title: IRC §1033 — Involuntary conversions
entries.summary: Qualifying proceeds from destroyed or condemned business/investment property may receive nonrecognition when reinvested in eligible replacement property under statutory conditions.
entries.details: The reading uses it for compensation for a destroyed building; examine detailed replacement requirements in statutory text.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: When qualifying property is destroyed or taken and you use the proceeds to buy suitable replacement property, tax law may let you delay reporting the gain.

entries.title: IRC §104(a)(2) — Physical injury or sickness damages
