entries.summary: Qualifying damages (other than punitive damages) received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness are excluded from gross income.
entries.details: Applies to qualifying damages whether recovered by suit or agreement and in lump-sum or periodic form; the causal link to physical injury/sickness is critical.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.examTrap: Nonphysical injury, reputational harm, or ordinary emotional distress does not by itself satisfy §104(a)(2). Punitive damages remain taxable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Money received as damages because of a physical injury or physical sickness can be tax-free, but punitive damages and many purely emotional-distress awards are different.

entries.title: Compensatory versus punitive damages
entries.summary: Compensatory damages replace an identified loss; punitive damages are imposed as punishment or deterrence.
entries.details: For tax consequences examine the origin and purpose of payment, any statutory exclusion, and whether a return of capital is involved.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.laymanExplanation: Compensatory damages aim to repay a loss. Punitive damages are an additional amount meant to punish the wrongdoer.

entries.title: Origin of the claim
entries.summary: The factual and legal nature of the underlying claim that gives rise to damages.
entries.details: Distinguish recoveries for lost profits, destroyed property, physical personal injury, and reputation/emotional harms.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.laymanExplanation: To classify lawsuit money for tax purposes, ask: 'What was this payment really for?' Lost wages, damaged property, and physical injury can have different tax outcomes.

entries.title: Murphy v. United States (Murphy II)
entries.summary: The D.C. Circuit held the award did not fall within §104(a)(2)'s physical-injury exclusion, was included in §61 gross income, and could constitutionally be taxed; the judgment was affirmed.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 80
entries.facts: Murphy received damages for emotional distress and harm to reputation after whistleblower complaints. Her recovery was not attributable to personal physical injury.
entries.issue: Whether emotional-distress/reputational damages are excluded by §104(a)(2), included by §61, and constitutionally taxable.
entries.holding: The D.C. Circuit held the award did not fall within §104(a)(2)'s physical-injury exclusion, was included in §61 gross income, and could constitutionally be taxed; the judgment was affirmed.
entries.reasoning: The 1996 statutory revision restricted the exclusion to physical injuries or sickness. Congress could tax this recovery through its Article I power; the tax was characterized as an excise on a transaction rather than an unapportioned direct ownership tax.
entries.rule: Analyze the injury's actual physical nature, the §104 statutory text, and whether the receipt replaces taxable income or falls within a specific exclusion. Do not cite the superseded earlier Murphy I opinion as controlling.

exam.source: Murphy v. United States, 493 F.3d 170 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (Murphy II), excerpt reproduced pp. 80–88

legalWarning.label: DISTINGUISH MURPHY I
legalWarning.reason: The chapter discusses Murphy I, an earlier opinion withdrawn on rehearing. Murphy II is the operative appellate decision excerpted here.

examApplication.source: Murphy v. United States, 493 F.3d 170 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (Murphy II), excerpt reproduced pp. 80–88

legalWarning.label: DISTINGUISH MURPHY I
legalWarning.reason: The chapter discusses Murphy I, an earlier opinion withdrawn on rehearing. Murphy II is the operative appellate decision excerpted here.

entries.laymanExplanation: A whistleblower received damages for emotional harm and damage to reputation, not physical injury. The appeals court ruled the money was taxable and that Congress could tax it.

entries.title: Direct tax and apportionment
entries.summary: The Constitution requires certain direct federal taxes to be apportioned by population among states, subject to the Sixteenth Amendment for income taxes.
entries.details: Murphy II discusses Article I and distinguishes taxes on property ownership from taxes on transactions or activities.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 85
entries.laymanExplanation: For some taxes, the Constitution requires each state's tax share to follow its population. Federal income taxes have an important constitutional exception.

entries.title: Article I taxing power and constitutional limits
entries.summary: Congress has broad Article I power to lay taxes; direct taxes require apportionment except to the extent the Sixteenth Amendment permits unapportioned income taxes.
entries.details: The reproduced Murphy II excerpt reasons that taxing its award can be an excise on a transaction, satisfying the constitutional framework.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 85
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress has broad power to tax, but constitutional limits can affect particular taxes. The classification of the tax matters.

entries.title: Perez v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The payments were taxable compensation, not excludable damages for personal physical injury.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Perez v. Commissioner, 144 T.C. 51 (2015), reproduced pp. 90–94
entries.facts: Perez underwent painful injections and egg retrieval procedures under contracts that paid her $20,000 for compliance with the procedure. The contracts disclaimed payment for eggs and allocated medical risks to Perez.
entries.issue: Does contractual compensation for undergoing a voluntary painful medical procedure count as excludable damages on account of personal physical injuries under §104(a)(2)?
entries.holding: No. The payments were taxable compensation, not excludable damages for personal physical injury.
entries.reasoning: Perez voluntarily agreed to the procedures in exchange for compensation; the clinic did not pay damages for a wrong or compensable injury. The regulation's removal of the formal tort-rights requirement did not turn voluntary contractual services payments into damages.
entries.rule: §104(a)(2) requires qualifying damages on account of personal physical injury/sickness; compensation under a bargained-for voluntary services contract is not automatically damages.
entries.exam: Distinguish contract compensation for voluntarily undergone procedures from a recovery for a legally compensable physical injury.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish contract compensation for voluntarily undergone procedures from a recovery for a legally compensable physical injury.
entries.laymanExplanation: A woman was paid to go through an egg-retrieval process. The court said this was payment under a voluntary contract, not tax-free injury damages.

entries.title: Structured settlement
entries.summary: A legal settlement that pays qualified damages over time rather than as a single lump sum.
entries.details: The textbook explains that qualifying periodic payments for physical injuries may receive special tax treatment, creating a timing advantage.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 94
entries.laymanExplanation: A structured settlement pays lawsuit compensation over time instead of in a single check.

entries.title: Periodic payments for personal physical injury
entries.summary: Under §104(a)(2), qualifying physical-injury damages may be excludable whether paid in a lump sum or periodic payments.
entries.details: Structured settlements require careful analysis of entitlement and economic control; the reading highlights favorable treatment of certain deferred-payment components.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 94
entries.laymanExplanation: Qualifying physical-injury compensation may remain excluded even when paid in installments, subject to the applicable rules.

entries.title: Policy rationale for physical injury exclusion
entries.summary: Compensation arguably restores lost physical well-being rather than creating a net economic gain.
entries.details: The text contrasts physical with emotional/reputational injuries and asks why nominally similar compensation can be taxed differently.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79

topics.title: F. Illegal Income
topics.description: Taxability of unlawful gains, claims of right and restitution.

entries.title: Illegal proceeds may be taxable gross income
entries.summary: Unlawful gains can constitute gross income under §61, even if the recipient may later be required to repay them.
entries.details: James v. United States is referenced for the general principle: receipt without consensual recognition of an obligation to repay and without restriction can be taxable.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 96
entries.examTrap: Illegal character of income does not remove it from §61.
entries.laymanExplanation: You don't get an income-tax exemption because the money came from something illegal. Stolen or embezzled money can be taxable.

entries.title: Claim of right
entries.summary: A taxpayer's practical dominion over funds, without an acknowledged limitation or consensual obligation to repay, may support current inclusion.
entries.details: The source compares typical embezzlement proceeds against loans or prompt secured repayment arrangements.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97
entries.laymanExplanation: If you receive money and can use it as your own without accepting a genuine duty to return it, tax law may treat you as having income right now.

entries.title: Obligation to repay
entries.summary: A recognized duty to return money, relevant to whether receipt is a taxable accession to wealth or nonincome borrowing.
entries.details: Do not mistake a purely subjective intention to repay for a legally and factually supported borrowing obligation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97
entries.laymanExplanation: Borrowing money usually isn't income because you have a real obligation to pay it back. An empty promise to repay may not be enough.

entries.title: Gilbert v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Second Circuit reversed the Tax Court; under its unusual facts, the withdrawals were not income when acquired.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 96
entries.facts: Gilbert, a corporation president and principal shareholder, withdrew nearly $1.96 million in company funds without advance authorization to meet stock-purchase margin calls. Shortly afterward, he gave demand promissory notes and secured them with assets exceeding the debt's value; the corporate board accepted the security but did not ratify his initial actions.
entries.issue: Were Gilbert's unauthorized withdrawals taxable embezzlement income when he intended and secured prompt repayment?
entries.holding: The Second Circuit reversed the Tax Court; under its unusual facts, the withdrawals were not income when acquired.
entries.reasoning: Unlike typical embezzlement, Gilbert recognized repayment obligations, reasonably expected to repay, believed the withdrawals would be approved, and promptly delivered adequate collateral. These facts distinguished James and Buff.
entries.rule: Carefully compare initial intent, recognized debt, prompt security, reasonable repayment ability, and corporation's response. Do not treat a general post hoc promise to repay as enough.

exam.source: Gilbert v. Commissioner, 552 F.2d 478 (2d Cir. 1977), reproduced pp. 96–98

examApplication.source: Gilbert v. Commissioner, 552 F.2d 478 (2d Cir. 1977), reproduced pp. 96–98

entries.laymanExplanation: A company executive took money without permission but promptly gave real security and acknowledged repayment. The court treated those unusual facts differently from ordinary embezzlement.

entries.title: James v. United States (supporting citation)
entries.summary: The textbook cites James for the general taxability of embezzled funds.
entries.details: James is referenced within Gilbert; it is not a separately reproduced assigned opinion in the supplied pages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97

topics.title: G. Gain on Sale of a Home
topics.description: Section 121 home-sale gain exclusion and limitations.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Principal residence exclusion
entries.summary: A qualifying taxpayer may exclude up to $250,000 of gain on sale of a principal residence, or generally $500,000 for qualifying joint filers.
entries.details: General rule: taxpayer owned and used the property as principal residence for at least two years during the five-year period ending at sale; subject to frequency, filing and other conditions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100
entries.elements: Ownership and principal residence use: generally 2 of the 5 years before sale. Standard cap: $250,000; qualifying MFJ cap: $500,000.
entries.examTrap: A vacation property does not qualify merely because it is owned for two years; the principal-residence use requirement matters.
entries.laymanExplanation: When you sell your main home, the law may let you leave a large portion of the profit out of income tax if you meet ownership and living-in-the-home requirements.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Joint-return conditions
entries.summary: A $500,000 exclusion for qualifying married joint filers generally requires meeting joint-return, use, ownership and other statutory requirements.
entries.details: The reading notes that both spouses must satisfy the use test, while the ownership condition can be satisfied under the statutory joint-filer rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.laymanExplanation: A married couple filing jointly may qualify for a higher home-sale exclusion, but they must satisfy extra conditions.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Once-every-two-years limit
entries.summary: A taxpayer generally cannot claim the full §121 exclusion if it was used on a different sale within the preceding two years.
entries.details: The reading discusses reduced exclusions when sales arise from qualifying changes in employment, health, or certain unforeseen circumstances.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.laymanExplanation: You generally cannot use the full main-home sale exclusion every year. The law usually requires a two-year gap, with some exceptions.

entries.title: Principal residence
entries.summary: The home that serves as the taxpayer's main residence for purposes of §121's use requirement.
entries.details: This characterization is factual and distinct from owning a secondary home or investment property.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100
entries.laymanExplanation: Your principal residence is the place that actually functions as your main home, not just any house you own.

entries.title: Taxable gain after §121 exclusion
entries.summary: Taxable gain = max(0, realized home-sale gain − allowable §121 exclusion).
entries.details: Textbook example: single taxpayer's $100,000-basis residence sold for $400,000; realized gain $300,000, $250,000 excluded, $50,000 taxable (assuming full eligibility).
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.examApplication: Compute realized gain first, then determine §121 eligibility and exclusion limit.
entries.laymanExplanation: First calculate profit from selling your home. Then subtract the part the law lets you exclude. The remaining amount may be taxable.

entries.title: Pre-1997 home-sale gain rules
entries.summary: Former §1034 allowed rollover-style gain deferral on reinvestment in another home; prior §121 had a one-time older-taxpayer exclusion.
entries.details: These rules are repealed and appear in the reading only to explain the current §121 regime.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 102

legalWarning.label: REPEALED PRE-1997 LAW
legalWarning.reason: The old §1034 rollover provision and previous one-time home-sale exclusion were superseded by the 1997 enactment of current §121.

topics.title: B. Gifts — §102 and United States v. Harris
topics.description: Syllabus handout, Chapter 3, The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, pp. 154–161. Only the supplied Gifts excerpt is incorporated; other Chapter 3 sections have not been provided.

entries.title: IRC §102(a) — gifts excluded from recipient's gross income
entries.summary: The value of property acquired by gift is generally excluded from the recipient's gross income.
entries.details: The court explains that gross income under §61 does not include gifts under §102(a). But calling a transfer a 'gift' or having a personal relationship is not decisive. Analyze the donor's actual intent and whether the transfer instead compensates for services or another economic exchange.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 155–157.
entries.elements: (1) Identify a transfer of property or money; (2) determine whether it was a genuine gift under the transferor-intent standard; (3) distinguish consideration, services, legal or moral obligation, or anticipated economic benefit. Civil tax consequences are separate from criminal willfulness.
entries.examApplication: In a fact pattern involving periodic transfers from a wealthy individual to a romantic partner, discuss what motivated the transfer and what the recipient understood; do not assume the payments are gifts or wages based on the relationship alone.
entries.examTrap: §102(a) addresses the recipient's income; potential donor-side gift-tax issues are separate. The Harris opinion did NOT definitively decide the civil tax treatment of every payment in such a relationship.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone genuinely gives you money or property as a gift, you generally don't include its value in income. But payment for work isn't made a gift just by calling it one.

entries.title: Donor's intent / transferor's intent
entries.summary: In determining whether a transfer qualifies as a gift, the transferor's purpose is the critical consideration.
entries.details: Harris quotes and applies the framework from Commissioner v. Duberstein (1960): gifts may arise from detached and disinterested generosity or impulses such as affection; transfers driven by compensation for services, legal or moral duty, or anticipated business benefit may be income. Apply the facts, not a rigid categorical rule.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 155, 157, 159.
entries.examApplication: Look to correspondence, conduct, returns, relationship circumstances, timing, and whether transfers were tied to particular services. A donor's gift-tax return is relevant but may not settle intent.
entries.examTrap: Duberstein is CITED within the reproduced Harris opinion; no separate Duberstein opinion was supplied in this handout, so it is supporting authority here—not a separate assigned case brief.
entries.laymanExplanation: To decide whether something is a gift, ask what the person giving it meant to do. Were they being generous, or paying for something?

entries.title: Gift versus compensation for services
entries.summary: A gift reflects the transferor's donative motive; compensation is paid for services, duties, or anticipated economic return.
entries.details: Harris discusses financial and property transfers in a long-term romantic relationship and warns against treating all such payments as necessarily taxable compensation or necessarily gifts. Specific payments for specified services may be different from support and gifts motivated by affection.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 155–160.
entries.examApplication: Suppose one payment is tied to a specific contractual service and another is an unrestricted present motivated by personal affection. Identify donor intent separately for each transfer.
entries.examTrap: Neither 'romantic relationship' nor 'regular payment' alone supplies a conclusive answer.
entries.laymanExplanation: A friend sending birthday money is different from someone paying you to provide a service. The reason for the transfer matters more than its label.

entries.title: Criminal tax willfulness
entries.summary: A criminal tax conviction for willful nonpayment or nonfiling requires proof of a voluntary, intentional violation of a known legal duty.
entries.details: Harris involves §§7201 and 7203. In the criminal setting, the prosecution must prove the relevant criminal elements, including willfulness, beyond a reasonable doubt. A genuinely unsettled legal duty and a good-faith belief may defeat willfulness even if tax treatment could be contested in civil proceedings.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 154–160.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish whether money is income for civil tax purposes from whether the recipient knowingly violated a clear legal duty and could be criminally convicted.
entries.examTrap: Uncertainty sufficient to prevent criminal conviction does not automatically mean the disputed receipt is an excluded gift.
entries.laymanExplanation: Criminal tax law generally requires more than a wrong return. The prosecution must prove the person intentionally violated a tax duty they knew they had.

entries.title: Criminal burden of proof versus civil tax determination
entries.summary: The government must establish the charged criminal tax offense beyond a reasonable doubt; civil taxability is a different question.
entries.details: In Harris, the court found the donor's purpose inadequately proved as to Conley and serious uncertainty about the tax classification as to Harris. The court stressed that the criminal law must provide fair warning before it may punish willful nonfiling or evasion.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 154–160.
entries.examApplication: When a question asks whether a tax charge can support criminal sanctions, discuss donor intent, taxpayer knowledge, and legal clarity separately from the likely civil treatment.
entries.examTrap: Do not transform a reversal for insufficient criminal proof into a positive civil tax holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: A civil tax disagreement and a criminal tax prosecution have different stakes. Proving someone deliberately committed a crime is harder than disputing a tax bill.

entries.title: Donor-side gift tax versus donee income tax
entries.summary: Federal gift tax generally concerns transfers by a donor; §102(a) addresses whether the recipient includes the gift as income.
entries.details: The opinion frames the transfers as potentially involving donor-side gift-tax consequences or donee-side income-tax obligations; the criminal cases concerned alleged income-tax violations by the two recipients. Amounts, exemptions, exclusions and liabilities require separate gift-tax statutory analysis.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 154–155.
entries.examTrap: The fact that an amount is outside the donee's gross income does not mean 'no tax issues exist'; it may implicate donor-side gift-tax rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: A true gift usually isn't income for the person who receives it, but the person giving it may face separate gift-tax rules.

entries.title: Letters offered to show belief, not necessarily their truth
entries.summary: A communication can be relevant to the recipient's state of mind without being offered as proof that its factual claims are true.
entries.details: Kritzik wrote Harris affectionate letters and described gifts. The court held the letters were relevant to Harris's good-faith belief about his purpose and therefore should not have been excluded as hearsay solely because the letters might be false. This is a supporting evidentiary point in the Tax opinion, not the central gift definition.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 156–157.
entries.examApplication: A taxpayer's beliefs and the words communicated to them can matter to criminal willfulness, even when the exact objective truth of the statements is disputed.

entries.title: United States v. Harris (7th Cir. 1991)
entries.summary: The Seventh Circuit reversed the convictions of Harris and Conley and ordered dismissal of their indictments; the government had not shown the criminal tax duty and willfulness needed for convictions.
entries.details: This is a reproduced judicial opinion in the assigned handout, not merely a citation. The handout also includes a separate concurrence by Judge Flaum expressing concern about an overly categorical approach to payments between romantic partners.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reproduced opinion 'United States v. Harris,' 942 F.2d 1125, at printed pp. 154–160; Judge Flaum's concurrence and notes through p. 161.
entries.facts: David Kritzik, a wealthy widower, gave Leigh Ann Conley and Lynnette Harris (twin sisters) substantial amounts of money and property during personal relationships. The government alleged they should have reported the transfers as taxable income; both were convicted in separate criminal trials. Conley's prosecution relied on inferences about the donor's intent. Harris attempted to introduce Kritzik's letters describing affection and gifts, but the district court excluded them.
entries.issue: Could the government sustain criminal tax convictions treating these transfers as taxable income when it had not proved donor intent, when Harris's evidence of her good-faith belief was excluded, and when relevant gift-versus-income law did not clearly establish criminal liability?
entries.holding: No. Conley's conviction was reversed because the government had not sufficiently shown Kritzik's intent and her knowledge. Harris's conviction was reversed because relevant letters should have been admitted to show good-faith belief and because the unclear tax law did not give fair warning sufficient for a willful criminal violation. The court ordered dismissal of both indictments.
entries.reasoning: Applying Duberstein, the court identified the transferor's intent as central to the gift inquiry. Gift-tax returns did not establish the nature of all transfers to Conley. For Harris, affectionate letters could affect her belief even if not true, and their exclusion denied evidence central to willfulness. Prior civil Tax Court cases indicated noncriminal gift treatment in comparable personal relationships; the law was too unclear for criminal sanctions. The opinion did not establish a categorical civil tax exemption for transfers between lovers. Judge Flaum concurred in the judgment but criticized the majority's broad language and favored case-by-case donor-intent analysis.
entries.rule: The §102(a) gift inquiry focuses on the transferor's motive under Duberstein; ambiguous civil tax classifications and failures to prove knowledge of a known duty can defeat criminal willfulness. Harris does not conclusively exempt all personal-relationship transfers from civil income tax.
entries.exam: When facing gifts-versus-income questions, analyze donor motive and any quid pro quo. If the hypothetical asks for criminal liability, separately analyze proof of willfulness and clarity of the legal duty. Do not equate absence of criminal liability with a holding that the amount was necessarily a civil-tax gift.
entries.examApplication: A wealthy individual gives recurring money and jewelry to a longtime romantic partner. Assess affection, potential payment for services, donor statements and gift returns. Then, if the recipient failed to file a return, explain why the government must independently show a known tax duty and intentional violation.
entries.examTrap: The court vacated criminal convictions; it did not decide the broad civil question that all such transfers are gifts. Duberstein is a cited case, not a separately reproduced case opinion in this upload.
entries.sourceRole: Dedicated assigned-case brief based on the reproduced judicial opinion in the handout.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two women received substantial money from a wealthy man. The court threw out their criminal tax convictions because the government had not adequately shown the necessary criminal tax violations; it did not say every romantic gift is tax-free.

entries.title: Judge Flaum's concurrence — avoid a categorical gift rule
entries.summary: Judge Flaum agreed criminal convictions should fall but objected to treating all long-term romantic transfers as categorically exempt.
entries.details: The concurrence stresses individualized donor intent under Duberstein and warns that some payments may be compensation for services even within a sustained personal relationship. He joined the judgment because the record was insufficient and the legal standards were uncertain.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 160–161.
entries.examTrap: This is a concurrence, not a majority holding establishing a bright-line taxable or exempt category.
